slides.label: Title
slides.narration: Open by motivating the transition from coordinates to vectors. Coordinates label points; vectors encode displacements. This upgrade lets us express operations like addition, scaling, and rotation directly on geometric objects rather than on their numerical addresses. Orient students to printed pages 65 through 87.

slides.label: Lecture Route
slides.narration: Preview the five themes: vector operations, linear independence and bases, inner products, the Cauchy-Schwarz and triangle inequalities, and rotations via matrices and complex numbers. Students should leave with a working understanding of the Euclidean inner product as the bridge between linear algebra and metric geometry.

slides.label: Vector Operations
slides.narration: Present vector addition and scalar multiplication geometrically. Addition is the parallelogram diagonal; scalar multiplication stretches or compresses along the direction. Emphasize that these operations are defined without coordinates and can be verified once coordinates are chosen.

slides.label: Linear Independence
slides.narration: Explain linear independence as the condition that no vector in a set is a combination of the others. In the plane, two linearly independent vectors form a basis: every other vector can be written uniquely as a linear combination. The standard basis gives the familiar coordinate axes.

slides.label: Inner Product
slides.narration: Introduce the inner product as the algebraic tool that measures angles and lengths. The formula is the sum of component products, but the geometric meaning is a projection: the inner product of u and v measures how much u points in the direction of v, scaled by their lengths.

slides.label: Cauchy-Schwarz
slides.narration: Derive the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality from the inner product. The inequality says the absolute value of the inner product is at most the product of the lengths, with equality only when the vectors are parallel. Present the triangle inequality as a consequence.

slides.label: Rotations
slides.narration: Show how rotation by angle theta acts as a linear map with matrix entries involving cosine and sine. Then present the complex-number viewpoint: multiplication by the unit complex number at angle theta performs the same rotation. The two descriptions are equivalent.

slides.label: Recap
slides.narration: Summarize the chapter by connecting vectors, inner products, inequalities, and rotations into a coherent linear-algebraic framework for Euclidean geometry. The inner product is the central object: it defines lengths, angles, orthogonality, and projections.
